rv.q: In a taut, timely and finely acted revival by American director Jordan Fein, a drama that might sound contrived and far-fetched becomes brilliantly gripping.

There is so much emotive power in Jordan Fein’s production, such extraordinary performances by Gelb and Chanda, and so many chilling parallels to current political indifference to the horrors around the world, that the play’s lack of internal coherence becomes irrelevant.

Right now, Sylvia’s hysterical paralysis feels like an intensely sane reaction to the world and Chanda’s rendering of her climactic speech (“where is Roosevelt? Where is England?!?”) is shatteringly powerful.
Full of powerful themes and brutally unvarnished emotion, this is a knotty, confronting piece, but it lacks the focus and tragic force of Miller’s better-known plays.
This is not, until its closing moments, a subtle play.
A fascinating and fitfully brilliant production of a fascinating and fitfully brilliant play, but Broken Glass needs to be handled a bit more delicately than The Crucible et al.
The play is unable to hide its clumsy blending of medical paralysis, European persecution and American malaise.
Broken Glass lacks the tight, exquisite structures of Miller’s best, the crackling charge of A View from the Bridge or Death of a Salesman, both revived here in recent years.
But anyone who has ever been irked by his moralising tendencies will find more to annoy them here.
But late works, including his 1994 play Broken Glass, now on at the Young Vic, can be a bit windy.
Fein's thoughtful direction holds and tightens the corkscrewing emotions and thoughts of the play in a production that is always gripping and often devastating.
A new production of any Arthur Miller play is always a cause for great celebration, and this version of Broken Glass is no exception.
It makes for uncomfortable and distracting viewing.
But his directing also has a tendency, especially at the climax, of underlining the play’s meaning a bit too loudly: Broken Glass really doesn’t need this exaggerated approach.

Miller’s interrogation of antisemitism isn’t not relevant, it’s just that the political symbolism is overcomplicated by its entanglement with sexuality making it hard to detect what best to glean from Broken Glass.
This is historical fiction located in a period of history that the author lived through.

Miller’s later works were a far cry from the heady output he achieved in his heyday, but there are occasional nuggets which remind us of his brilliance, my personal favourite being The Last Yankee completed around the same time.
It is staged relatively rarely compared to Miller’s major plays which include Death of a Salesman, The Crucible and A View From the Bridge.
For that line, everything is forgiven.
There is nothing wrong with fine, but it does stop just shy of becoming as thrilling and compelling as it promises to be.
There are moments to admire in this production, but it doesn't quite connect with its themes of antisemitism, overwork, sexuality, and political inertia.

cn.t: Miller's 1994 drama feels timely amid rising antisemitism, but critics find it meandering and uneven compared to his masterpieces. Strong performances and hypnotic moments can't fully overcome the play's repetitive structure.
